First observe whether you can record an incident according to procedure, listen calmly and clarify authority; then check whether you can accept shifts, outdoor work and the actual recruitment conditions. Career exploration is not the same as hiring, appointment or enforcement authorisation. Interest, record ability, real arrangements and formal qualification have to be checked separately.

Behaviour suited to further exploration includes: being able to separate what you saw from what others said, keep a timeline, and be willing to correct an initial judgement; at handover, stating what has not yet been verified and feeding it back to the corresponding responsible person. Faced with uncertain information, do not fill in facts on your own, and when challenged, still be able to explain the basis.

Situations needing caution include: liking only exciting scenes, resisting paperwork and review, treating another person's complaint as an offence, or being willing to substitute guesswork for checking authority. Police officers may work with station staff, dispatch and other law enforcement agencies, and the actual duties are divided by organisation. When the incident jurisdiction or authority to act needs confirming, report to the responsible person with authority, and do not take over other duties just because you are at the same scene.

The United States occupational material describes patrol, investigation and safety coordination; the police and detectives broad group commonly has full-time shifts. The P3 handover should carry the timeline, the information sources, the known actions and the unchecked items; the material is only a fictional exercise and contains no real personal data. The receipt and disclosure of real incident records must follow organisational rules.

Patrol and incident recording connect to each other: the former focuses on order and safety in the transit area, and the latter preserves observations, reports and follow-up verification.
